options.text: Show the child detailed anatomical diagrams of the throat several days before surgery.
options.why: Abstract diagrams and long lead times suit older school-age children and adolescents; a preschooler cannot use this information and may fantasize during the wait.

options.text: Let the child handle the anesthesia mask and act out the procedure on a doll, using simple, concrete words shortly before surgery.
options.why: Preschoolers are preoperational: egocentric, concrete, prone to magical thinking, and with a limited sense of time. Therapeutic play with real equipment and simple, honest words given close to the event reduces fear.

options.text: Tell the child that the doctor will "put you to sleep" during the operation.
options.why: Preschoolers interpret words literally and may connect "put to sleep" with a pet that died; say "a special sleep medicine so you won't feel anything, and you will wake up."

options.text: Discuss how the surgery will affect the child's appearance in front of friends.
options.why: Concern about body image and peer opinion is typical of adolescents, not preschoolers.

takeaway: Preschoolers think concretely and literally: prepare them shortly before procedures with play, dolls, and real equipment in simple words.

stem: The parent of a 2-month-old asks when the child should receive the first dose of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Which response by the nurse is accurate according to the CDC schedule?

options.text: Today, along with the other 2-month vaccines
options.why: MMR is not part of the 2-month vaccines (which include DTaP, IPV, Hib, PCV, hepatitis B, and rotavirus).

options.text: At 12 to 15 months of age, with a second dose at 4 to 6 years
options.why: The routine CDC schedule gives MMR dose 1 at 12–15 months and dose 2 at 4–6 years. Maternal antibodies can interfere with the response before 12 months.

options.text: At 6 months of age, with a booster at 12 months
options.why: An early dose at 6–11 months is given only before international travel or during an outbreak, and it does not count toward the routine 2-dose series.

options.text: Only once, at school entry at 4 to 6 years
options.why: MMR is a 2-dose series; waiting until school entry leaves the toddler unprotected against measles.

takeaway: MMR (live vaccine): dose 1 at 12–15 months, dose 2 at 4–6 years.

stem: A 12-month-old is due for the MMR and varicella vaccines. Which finding should cause the nurse to hold the vaccines and consult the provider?

options.text: The child has mild diarrhea and a temperature of 37.8°C (100°F).
options.why: A mild illness with or without low-grade fever is not a reason to delay vaccination; only moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution.

options.text: The child developed hives after eating scrambled eggs.
options.why: Egg allergy is not a contraindication to MMR; the vaccine is grown in chick embryo cell culture with negligible egg protein, so it can be given routinely.

options.text: The child's mother is 5 months pregnant.
options.why: A pregnant household contact is not a contraindication; MMR viruses are not transmitted from vaccinated people, and the CDC states that varicella vaccine may also be given.

options.text: The child is receiving chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
options.why: MMR and varicella are live vaccines and are contraindicated in severely immunocompromised children, such as those receiving chemotherapy.

takeaway: Live vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus) are withheld in severe immunosuppression; mild illness and egg allergy are not contraindications.

stem: A nurse is reviewing the vital signs of a 2-month-old infant who is sleeping quietly. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Heart rate of 138/min
options.why: Normal infant heart rate is about 90–160/min asleep (up to about 180/min awake), so 138/min is expected.

options.text: Axillary temperature of 36.9°C (98.4°F)
options.why: This temperature is within normal limits.

options.text: Respiratory rate of 68/min
options.why: A sleeping infant's respiratory rate is normally about 30–53/min; a rate of 60/min or more in a young infant is tachypnea and may signal respiratory distress or sepsis.

options.text: Blood pressure of 78/46 mmHg
options.why: Normal infant systolic blood pressure is about 72–104 mmHg, so this reading is expected.

takeaway: In infants, a respiratory rate of 60/min or more at rest is tachypnea and needs to be reported.

stem: A 9-month-old infant has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Which assessment finding indicates severe dehydration that needs immediate intervention?

options.text: Dry mucous membranes and decreased tears when crying
options.why: These are signs of mild to moderate dehydration; they need oral rehydration and monitoring, but they are not the most urgent finding.

options.text: Heart rate of 150/min while crying
options.why: A heart rate of 150/min in a crying infant is within normal limits; worsening tachycardia at rest would be more concerning.

options.text: Lethargy, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and cool, mottled extremities
options.why: Altered mental status, delayed capillary refill (more than 3 seconds), and cool, mottled skin show poor perfusion from severe dehydration (early hypovolemic shock). This requires rapid isotonic IV fluid boluses.

options.text: Four wet diapers in the past 24 hours, slightly fewer than usual
options.why: Mildly reduced urine output is consistent with mild dehydration, not severe dehydration.

takeaway: Severe dehydration in infants = lethargy, capillary refill over 3 seconds, cool mottled skin, and minimal urine output; treat with IV isotonic boluses.

stem: A provider prescribes amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day orally, divided every 12 hours, for a child with acute otitis media. The child weighs 22 lb. How many milligrams should the nurse give per dose?

options.text: 225 mg
options.why: This divides the daily dose into 4 doses (every 6 hours) instead of 2 doses every 12 hours.

options.text: 450 mg
options.why: 22 lb ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg. 90 mg/kg/day × 10 kg = 900 mg/day. Divided every 12 hours (2 doses) = 450 mg per dose.

options.text: 900 mg
options.why: This is the total daily dose; giving it every 12 hours would double the prescribed amount.

options.text: 990 mg
options.why: This uses the weight in pounds (22 × 90 = 1,980 mg ÷ 2), which overdoses the child by more than double.

takeaway: Always convert pounds to kilograms (÷ 2.2), calculate the daily dose, and then divide by the number of doses per day.

stem: A provider prescribes acetaminophen 15 mg/kg orally every 6 hours as needed for fever for a child who weighs 18 kg. The available oral suspension is 160 mg/5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give per dose? (Round to the nearest tenth.)

options.text: 1.7 mL
options.why: This is 270 ÷ 160 without multiplying by 5 mL, which forgets the volume the concentration refers to and underdoses the child.

options.text: 5.6 mL
options.why: This volume equals 10 mg/kg (180 mg), not the prescribed 15 mg/kg.

options.text: 8.4 mL
options.why: 15 mg/kg × 18 kg = 270 mg. 270 mg ÷ 160 mg × 5 mL = 8.44 mL, which rounds to 8.4 mL. A dose of 15 mg/kg is within the safe single dose for children.
This volume equals 30 mg/kg (540 mg), twice the prescribed dose, which puts the child at risk for liver toxicity.

takeaway: Desired dose (mg/kg × kg) ÷ concentration (mg) × volume (mL) = mL to give; check every result against the mg/kg order.

stem: A child who weighs 16 kg has a skin infection. The provider prescribes cephalexin 300 mg orally every 8 hours. The facility's drug reference lists a safe dose of 25–50 mg/kg/day, divided every 6 to 12 hours, for this infection. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give the dose, because 300 mg is within the safe daily range of 400–800 mg.
options.why: This compares a single dose with a daily range. The daily total (900 mg) is what must be compared, and it exceeds 800 mg.

options.text: Give the dose, because the order is below the safe range and will not cause toxicity.
options.why: The order is above the safe range, not below it; this misreads the calculation.

options.text: Give 266 mg instead, so that the daily total equals the 800 mg maximum.
options.why: Nurses cannot independently change a prescribed dose; an unsafe order must be clarified with the provider.

options.text: Hold the dose and contact the provider, because the prescribed 900 mg/day exceeds the safe maximum of 800 mg/day.
options.why: Safe range: 25 × 16 = 400 mg/day to 50 × 16 = 800 mg/day. Prescribed: 300 mg × 3 doses = 900 mg/day, which is above the maximum. The nurse must clarify the order before giving the drug.

takeaway: Safe-dose check: (mg/kg/day low and high) × weight in kg; compare the prescribed TOTAL daily dose, and clarify any order outside the range.

stem: A 3-month-old with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) bronchiolitis has copious nasal secretions, is feeding poorly, has a respiratory rate of 56/min, and has an SpO2 of 94% on room air. Which nursing intervention is the priority?

options.text: Administer albuterol nebulizer treatments every 4 hours.
options.why: The AAP recommends against routine bronchodilators for bronchiolitis because they do not improve outcomes.

options.text: Gently suction the nares before feedings and as needed.
options.why: Young infants breathe mainly through the nose; clearing secretions improves air entry and the ability to feed. Supportive care (suctioning, hydration, oxygen only if needed) is the AAP-recommended treatment.

options.text: Perform chest physiotherapy every 4 hours.
options.why: The AAP recommends against chest physiotherapy in bronchiolitis; it adds distress and has no proven benefit.

options.text: Apply oxygen to keep the SpO2 at 98% or higher.
options.why: The AAP supports supplemental oxygen when SpO2 stays below 90%; 94% does not require oxygen, and aiming for 98% or higher is unnecessary.

takeaway: Bronchiolitis care is supportive: nasal suctioning, hydration, oxygen if SpO2 below 90%, and contact precautions; avoid routine albuterol, steroids, and chest physiotherapy.

stem: A 3-year-old with an incomplete immunization history has a sudden fever of 39.8°C (103.6°F), drooling, a muffled voice, and inspiratory stridor, and is sitting upright leaning forward with the chin thrust out. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Inspect the throat with a tongue blade to assess the epiglottis.
options.why: Inserting a tongue blade or swab can cause laryngospasm and total airway obstruction in epiglottitis; the throat is examined only where an emergency airway can be secured.

options.text: Keep the child upright on the parent's lap, avoid examining the throat, and prepare emergency airway equipment.
options.why: These findings suggest epiglottitis. Agitation or a throat exam can cause complete airway obstruction. Keep the child calm in a position of comfort and have intubation or tracheostomy equipment ready.

options.text: Place the child supine for a lateral neck x-ray.
options.why: Lying the child flat can worsen obstruction; a child with suspected epiglottitis should stay upright and be closely attended.

options.text: Give cool mist and oral dexamethasone as for croup.
options.why: Croup usually starts gradually with a barking cough and no drooling; this sudden, toxic picture with drooling is epiglottitis, an airway emergency.

takeaway: Epiglottitis (the 4 Ds: drooling, dysphagia, dysphonia, distress, plus tripod position): no throat exam, keep upright and calm, and prepare for airway support.

stem: A 9-year-old is being treated for an acute asthma exacerbation. Earlier, the child had loud expiratory wheezes throughout. Which finding now is most concerning to the nurse?

options.text: Markedly diminished breath sounds with no audible wheeze, and the child is drowsy.
options.why: A "silent chest" means air movement is so poor that wheezes can no longer be heard; together with drowsiness, it signals impending respiratory failure and needs emergency intervention.

options.text: Audible expiratory wheeze with a peak flow of 65% of personal best
options.why: This shows a moderate exacerbation; it needs treatment, but there is still air movement.

options.text: Coughing that produces clear mucus
options.why: A productive cough is common during asthma exacerbations and may show that secretions are clearing.

options.text: Heart rate of 118/min after an albuterol treatment
options.why: Tachycardia is an expected side effect of albuterol and is acceptable in this situation.

takeaway: In asthma, a quiet chest in a tiring or drowsy child is an ominous sign of respiratory failure, not improvement.

stem: A nurse is teaching the parent of a 4-year-old with cystic fibrosis about pancrelipase capsules. Which statement by the parent indicates understanding?

options.text: "I will crush the capsules and mix them into a bottle of milk."
options.why: Crushing the enteric-coated beads or mixing them into milk or other dairy foods breaks down the coating; the capsule may be opened and the beads sprinkled on a small amount of acidic soft food such as applesauce and swallowed without chewing.

options.text: "I will give the whole day's capsules once daily at bedtime."
options.why: Enzymes taken without food do not help digestion; they must be given with each meal and snack.

options.text: "I will give the capsules at the start of every meal and snack."
options.why: Pancreatic enzymes must be present with food to digest fat and protein, so they are taken with every meal and snack.

options.text: "I will cut back on the capsules if the stools become greasy and frequent."
options.why: Bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhea) suggest the dose is too low; the parent should report this so the provider can adjust the dose.

takeaway: Cystic fibrosis: pancreatic enzymes with every meal and snack, not crushed or chewed; steatorrhea means the dose is too low.

stem: A 7-month-old is choking on a piece of food. The infant is conscious but cannot cry or cough. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Give 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts, with the infant's head lower than the chest.
options.why: For a conscious choking infant under 1 year old, the AHA recommends cycles of 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object comes out or the infant becomes unresponsive.

options.text: Give abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled.
options.why: Abdominal thrusts are used for children over 1 year old and adults; in infants they can injure the abdominal organs.

options.text: Perform a blind finger sweep of the infant's mouth.
options.why: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove an object only if it can be seen.

options.text: Begin chest compressions at a rate of 100–120/min.
options.why: CPR is started only if the infant becomes unresponsive; this infant is still conscious.

takeaway: Conscious choking infant: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts; abdominal thrusts are for children over 1 year old.

stem: A 10-month-old with unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot becomes irritable while crying, then suddenly develops deep cyanosis and rapid, deep breathing. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Place the infant in a knee-chest position.
options.why: During a hypercyanotic ("tet") spell, the knee-chest position increases systemic vascular resistance and reduces right-to-left shunting, which sends more blood to the lungs. Calming the infant, oxygen, and IV morphine may follow.

options.text: Place the infant in a high Fowler's position.
options.why: An upright position does not raise systemic vascular resistance and does not reduce the shunt.

options.text: Obtain a 12-lead ECG.
options.why: An ECG does not treat the spell and would delay the immediate, positional intervention.

options.text: Lay the infant flat with the legs straight.
options.why: A flat position does not increase systemic vascular resistance; flexing the knees to the chest is what improves blood flow to the lungs.

takeaway: Tet spell: knee-chest position first (older children squat), then calm the child, give oxygen, and give morphine as prescribed.

stem: A 3-year-old with Kawasaki disease received IV immune globulin (IVIG) and is being discharged on low-dose aspirin. Which statement by the parent indicates understanding of discharge teaching?

options.text: "I can give ibuprofen for fever along with the aspirin."
options.why: Ibuprofen blocks aspirin's antiplatelet effect and should be avoided in children taking aspirin for Kawasaki disease.

options.text: "Once the fever is gone, my child's heart is no longer at risk."
options.why: Coronary artery aneurysms can develop in the weeks after the illness; follow-up echocardiograms are required.

options.text: "If my child is exposed to flu or chickenpox, there is no need to call."
options.why: Children taking aspirin are at risk for Reye syndrome with influenza or varicella; parents should report exposures, and an annual inactivated flu vaccine is recommended.

options.text: "My child should wait about 11 months after IVIG before getting the MMR and varicella vaccines."
options.why: Antibodies in IVIG can stop live vaccines from working; the CDC recommends delaying MMR and varicella for about 11 months after high-dose IVIG.

takeaway: Kawasaki disease: IVIG plus aspirin, follow-up echocardiograms for coronary aneurysms, delay live vaccines about 11 months after IVIG, and report flu or varicella exposure.

stem: A 5-week-old infant has projectile, nonbilious vomiting after feedings, seems hungry right after vomiting, and has a palpable olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen. Which laboratory finding should the nurse expect?

options.text: Metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia
options.why: Acidosis is associated with diarrhea or poor perfusion, not with loss of gastric acid.

options.text: Respiratory acidosis with hypercapnia
options.why: Pyloric stenosis is not a respiratory problem; its acid-base disturbance is metabolic.

options.text: Hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia
options.why: Repeated vomiting of stomach contents causes loss of hydrochloric acid and potassium, which leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. This must be corrected before pyloromyotomy.

options.text: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis
options.why: This pattern comes from loss of bicarbonate, such as with diarrhea, which is the opposite of losing gastric acid.

takeaway: Pyloric stenosis: projectile nonbilious vomiting, olive-shaped mass, hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis; correct fluids and electrolytes before surgery.

stem: A 10-month-old with intermittent colicky abdominal pain, knees drawn to the chest, and currant jelly-like stools is scheduled for an air enema reduction of intussusception. Before the procedure, the infant passes a normal brown stool. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Continue preparing the infant for the procedure as scheduled.
options.why: Going ahead without telling the provider ignores a finding that may make the procedure unnecessary.

options.text: Offer oral fluids, because bowel function has returned.
options.why: The infant should stay NPO until the provider evaluates the infant; reduction has not been confirmed.

options.text: Document the stool as an expected finding before the enema.
options.why: A normal stool is not expected with an obstructing intussusception; it is significant and must be reported.

options.text: Notify the provider of the stool immediately.
options.why: A normal brown stool may mean the intussusception has reduced on its own. The provider needs to know, because this may change the diagnostic and treatment plan.

takeaway: Intussusception: currant jelly stools and a sausage-shaped mass; a normal brown stool before reduction may mean it reduced on its own, so report it.

stem: An 18-month-old with Hirschsprung disease is awaiting a pull-through procedure. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Chronic constipation with ribbon-like stools
options.why: Ribbon-like stools and chronic constipation are expected features of Hirschsprung disease.

options.text: Fever, abdominal distension, and explosive, foul-smelling watery diarrhea
options.why: These signs suggest Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, a life-threatening complication that can quickly cause sepsis and shock.

options.text: Weight in the 10th percentile with poor appetite
options.why: Poor growth is common with Hirschsprung disease and is a concern, but it is not urgent.

options.text: A palpable fecal mass in the left lower abdomen
options.why: Retained stool is expected because the aganglionic segment cannot move stool forward.

takeaway: Hirschsprung disease: delayed meconium (more than 48 hours) and ribbon-like stools; fever plus explosive diarrhea and distension = enterocolitis, an emergency.

stem: An 11-year-old with suspected appendicitis has had right lower quadrant pain for 18 hours and is awaiting surgery. The child suddenly tells the nurse that the pain is "all better." Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Document the improvement and ask the provider whether the child can be discharged.
options.why: Treating sudden relief as improvement misses a possible perforation.

options.text: Apply a heating pad to the abdomen for comfort.
options.why: Heat increases blood flow and can speed rupture; heat is contraindicated with suspected appendicitis.

options.text: Assess for signs of peritonitis, such as a rigid abdomen, fever, and tachycardia, and notify the surgeon.
options.why: A sudden relief of pain may mean the appendix has perforated, with peritonitis soon following. The nurse should assess and report immediately.

options.text: Give a prescribed stool softener, because constipation may have caused the pain.
options.why: Laxatives and enemas can increase peristalsis and cause perforation; they are avoided when appendicitis is suspected.

takeaway: In appendicitis, sudden relief of pain suggests perforation; assess for peritonitis and report. Avoid heat, laxatives, and enemas.

stem: A nurse is comparing two children with edema. Which finding supports a diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome rather than acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?

options.text: Serum albumin of 1.6 g/dL with heavy proteinuria and elevated cholesterol
options.why: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, and generalized edema, usually with normal blood pressure.

options.text: Cola-colored urine
options.why: Gross hematuria (tea- or cola-colored urine) is typical of nephritic disease such as poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

options.text: Blood pressure of 140/92 mmHg
options.why: Hypertension from fluid and sodium retention is a key feature of acute glomerulonephritis; blood pressure is usually normal or low in minimal change nephrotic syndrome.

options.text: Elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer
options.why: An elevated ASO titer shows recent group A streptococcal infection, which supports poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

takeaway: Nephrotic = massive proteinuria, low albumin, high lipids, marked edema. Nephritic = hematuria, hypertension, mild edema, often after strep.

stem: A nurse is teaching the parents of an 18-month-old who had a simple febrile seizure. Which statement by a parent indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If another seizure happens, I will lay my child on one side and not put anything in the mouth."
options.why: This is correct seizure first aid that protects the airway.

options.text: "I will call 911 if a seizure lasts longer than 5 minutes."
options.why: This is correct; a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes needs emergency treatment.

options.text: "I will give fever medicine around the clock so that another seizure cannot happen."
options.why: The AAP notes that antipyretics make the child more comfortable but do not prevent febrile seizures; around-the-clock dosing also increases the risk of overdose.

options.text: "Most children outgrow febrile seizures by about age 5."
options.why: This is accurate; febrile seizures usually occur between 6 months and 5 years and generally do not cause lasting harm.

takeaway: Simple febrile seizures are benign; antipyretics give comfort but do not prevent recurrence. Call EMS for a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes.

stem: An 8-month-old is admitted with suspected bacterial meningitis. The infant has a fever, a bulging fontanel, irritability, and a high-pitched cry. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Place the infant on droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy is complete.
options.why: Bacterial meningitis (such as meningococcal) spreads by respiratory droplets; droplet precautions are kept until 24 hours after effective antibiotics have started.

options.text: Place the infant in an airborne-infection isolation room.
options.why: Airborne precautions are for illnesses such as measles, varicella, and tuberculosis, not bacterial meningitis.

options.text: Rely on Kernig and Brudzinski signs to confirm the diagnosis.
options.why: These signs are often absent in infants; a bulging fontanel, irritability, poor feeding, and a high-pitched cry are more reliable signs in this age group.

options.text: Hold the antibiotic until the cerebrospinal fluid culture results are available.
options.why: Antibiotics must not be delayed for culture results; cultures are obtained, ideally before the first dose, but treatment starts right away.

takeaway: Bacterial meningitis: droplet precautions for 24 hours after antibiotics start; infants show a bulging fontanel and high-pitched cry rather than nuchal rigidity.

stem: A 7-month-old with hydrocephalus has a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Which finding indicates a late sign of increased intracranial pressure that requires immediate action?

options.text: Irritability and poor feeding
options.why: These are early, nonspecific signs of increased intracranial pressure; they should be reported but are not late signs.

options.text: Bradycardia, irregular respirations, and a widening pulse pressure
options.why: Cushing triad is a late sign of increased intracranial pressure and suggests impending brain herniation; in a child with a shunt, it strongly suggests shunt malfunction and needs emergency intervention.

options.text: A full, tense fontanel when the infant is calm and upright
options.why: A bulging fontanel is an early sign of increased intracranial pressure in infants whose sutures have not closed.

options.text: Head circumference increased by 0.5 cm in the past month
options.why: Head growth of about 0.5 cm per month is expected at this age; rapid or excessive growth would be concerning.

takeaway: Infant increased ICP: early signs are bulging fontanel, irritability, high-pitched cry, sunset eyes, and growing head circumference; late signs are Cushing triad (bradycardia, irregular respirations, widening pulse pressure).

stem: A 12-year-old with sickle cell disease is admitted for a vaso-occlusive crisis and is receiving IV fluids and morphine by PCA. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider first?

options.text: Leg pain rated 6 on a 0–10 scale while using the PCA
options.why: Ongoing pain is expected in a crisis and calls for reassessing the pain plan, but it is less urgent than respiratory compromise.

options.text: Urine output of 1.2 mL/kg/hr
options.why: This is adequate urine output and shows that hydration is effective.

options.text: New chest pain, temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F), respiratory rate of 32/min, and SpO2 of 89%
options.why: These signs suggest acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death in sickle cell disease. It needs urgent oxygen, antibiotics, and possibly transfusion.

options.text: Yellow sclerae
options.why: Mild jaundice is common in sickle cell disease because of chronic hemolysis.

takeaway: In sickle cell crisis, watch for acute chest syndrome (chest pain, fever, hypoxemia, new infiltrate); incentive spirometry helps prevent it.

stem: A 6-year-old with hemophilia A falls and develops a painful, swollen, warm right knee. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Apply warm compresses to the knee.
options.why: Heat causes vasodilation and can increase bleeding; cold is used during acute bleeding.

options.text: Begin range-of-motion exercises to prevent stiffness.
options.why: Moving the joint during an acute bleed worsens bleeding; immobilize first, and start physical therapy after the bleeding is controlled.

options.text: Give ibuprofen for the pain.
options.why: NSAIDs and aspirin impair platelet function and increase bleeding risk; acetaminophen is preferred.

options.text: Give the prescribed factor VIII concentrate.
options.why: Prompt factor VIII replacement stops bleeding into the joint and limits long-term joint damage; rest, ice, and immobilization support it. Acetaminophen is used for pain.

takeaway: Hemophilia joint bleed: give factor replacement first plus RICE; avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, IM injections, and rectal temperatures.

stem: A 5-year-old with acute lymphoblastic leukemia has an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of 380/mm³. Which action should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.text: Take the child's temperature rectally every 4 hours.
options.why: Rectal temperatures can injure the mucosa and introduce bacteria; they are avoided in neutropenic children.

options.text: Allow a cousin with a cold to visit if the cousin wears a mask.
options.why: Anyone with an active infection should not visit a severely neutropenic child.

options.text: Place fresh flowers from the family at the bedside.
options.why: Fresh flowers and standing water can carry bacteria and fungi; most facilities do not allow them for neutropenic clients.

options.text: Provide a private room and require strict hand hygiene for everyone who enters.
options.why: An ANC below 500/mm³ is severe neutropenia; a private room and careful hand hygiene are the most important protections against infection.

takeaway: ANC below 500/mm³ = severe neutropenia: private room, hand hygiene, no sick visitors, no rectal temperatures or fresh flowers, and report fever right away.

stem: A 4-year-old with varicella (chickenpox) is admitted with a secondary skin infection. Which type of isolation should the nurse implement?

options.text: Standard precautions only
options.why: Standard precautions alone do not prevent airborne spread of varicella.

options.text: Airborne and contact precautions in a negative-pressure room
options.why: Varicella spreads by airborne particles and by direct contact with lesions; both precautions are kept until all lesions are crusted over.

options.text: Droplet precautions in a private room
options.why: Varicella travels through the air beyond the short droplet range, so droplet precautions are not enough.

options.text: Contact precautions only
options.why: Contact precautions alone do not protect against airborne spread.

takeaway: Varicella: airborne + contact precautions until all lesions are crusted; only immune staff should provide care.

stem: A 2-year-old has a blood lead level of 25 mcg/dL. The family lives in a house built in 1950 with peeling paint. Which statement by the parent indicates understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I will sand the peeling paint off the walls myself this weekend."
options.why: Sanding or scraping lead paint creates dangerous dust; abatement should be done by certified professionals while the child is away from the home.

options.text: "I will limit foods high in iron and calcium."
options.why: Iron and calcium reduce lead absorption, so the diet should include more of these foods, not less.

options.text: "I will wet-mop the floors and wipe the windowsills with a damp cloth often."
options.why: Wet cleaning removes lead dust without spreading it into the air; leaded paint in homes built before 1978 is the main source of exposure.

options.text: "I will use hot tap water for cooking and mixing formula."
options.why: Hot water draws more lead from old pipes; cold, flushed water should be used.

takeaway: Lead poisoning prevention: wet-clean dust, use professional abatement, eat more iron and calcium, and use cold tap water; old paint (before 1978) is the main source.

stem: A 14-month-old is brought to the emergency department with burns on both feet and ankles that have a sharp, even line of demarcation and no splash marks. The parent states the child climbed into the bathtub alone. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Confront the parent about the inconsistent history.
options.why: Confrontation can raise the risk to the child and interfere with the investigation; the nurse documents objectively and reports.

options.text: Wait for the provider to confirm abuse before making a report.
options.why: The duty to report belongs to each mandated reporter individually and does not require confirmation by the provider.

options.text: Report the suspected abuse to child protective services according to state law and agency policy.
options.why: Symmetric stocking-pattern burns without splash marks suggest forced immersion. Nurses are mandated reporters, and reasonable suspicion, not proof, is enough to report.

options.text: Discharge the child with burn care teaching and a follow-up visit.
options.why: Sending the child home without reporting may return the child to an unsafe environment.

takeaway: Suspect abuse when an injury does not match the history or the child's development (immersion burns, patterned bruises); nurses must report suspicion; proof is not required.

stem: A 3-year-old is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after possibly swallowing an unknown number of acetaminophen tablets. The child is alert and playful, with normal vital signs. The parent asks, "She seems fine. Can we go home?" Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "We will give syrup of ipecac to make her vomit the tablets."
options.why: Ipecac is no longer recommended; it delays definitive treatment and creates a risk of aspiration.

options.text: "Because she has no symptoms, she can safely go home with instructions."
options.why: Having no symptoms early does not rule out a toxic ingestion; discharging without a level could miss liver failure.

options.text: "Acetylcysteine is given only if she becomes jaundiced."
options.why: Acetylcysteine works best when started within 8 hours; waiting for jaundice means liver injury has already occurred.

options.text: "Liver damage may not show for a day or more. A blood level drawn 4 hours after the ingestion will show whether she needs the antidote, acetylcysteine."
options.why: Acetaminophen toxicity often causes few or no early symptoms; liver injury appears 24–72 hours later. The 4-hour serum level plotted on the nomogram guides acetylcysteine treatment. Activated charcoal may be given early if the child is alert and can protect the airway.

takeaway: Acetaminophen overdose: the child may look well early; get a 4-hour level and give acetylcysteine (best within 8 hours) to prevent liver failure.

stem: A 16-year-old at a clinic asks to be tested for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and says, "Please don't tell my parents." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.text: "I will need to call one of your parents to get consent before testing."
options.why: Parental consent is not required for minors' STI care; requiring it would discourage the teen from getting care.

options.text: "You can consent to STI testing and treatment yourself, and your information will be kept confidential. I encourage you to involve an adult you trust."
options.why: All U.S. states allow minors to consent to STI testing and treatment. Confidentiality encourages adolescents to seek care, and the only limits are situations of serious risk, such as abuse or danger to self or others.

options.text: "Confidentiality applies only to clients who are 18 or older."
options.why: Minors have confidentiality rights for specific services, including STI care; this statement is incorrect.

options.text: "We can test you, but your parents will receive a copy of the results."
options.why: Sharing results without the adolescent's permission breaks confidentiality and violates minor-consent laws.

takeaway: Adolescents can consent confidentially to STI care in every U.S. state; confidentiality can be broken only for risk of serious harm, such as abuse or suicidality.

stem: A nurse is preparing to start an IV on a 3-year-old. The parent asks, "Can I stay with my child?" Which response by the nurse reflects family-centered care?

options.text: "It is best if you wait outside so your child does not connect you with pain."
options.why: This idea is outdated; separation from parents increases a toddler's or preschooler's anxiety.

options.text: "Yes, please stay. You can hold your child's hand and talk to them during the procedure."
options.why: Family-centered care respects the parent as a partner; a parent's presence and comfort reduce a young child's distress and fear of separation.

options.text: "Parents are not allowed in the room during procedures."
options.why: Leaving parents out goes against family-centered care; parents should be allowed to choose whether to stay.

options.text: "We will do the IV in your child's bed so your child is more comfortable."
options.why: Painful procedures should be done in a treatment room so the bed and playroom stay safe places.

takeaway: Family-centered care: invite parents to stay and comfort the child during procedures, and do painful procedures in a treatment room, not in the child's bed.

stem: A nurse needs to assess pain in a 2-year-old after surgery. The child cannot yet reliably rate pain. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?

options.text: FLACC scale (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability)
options.why: FLACC is a behavioral scale validated for children about 2 months to 7 years old who cannot self-report pain, as well as for nonverbal children.

options.text: Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale
options.why: FACES requires the child to self-report and is generally used for children 3 years and older.

options.text: Numeric rating scale from 0 to 10
options.why: Numeric scales require an understanding of numbers and are used for children about 8 years and older.

options.text: CRIES scale
options.why: CRIES is designed for neonates in the postoperative period, not toddlers.

takeaway: Pain tools: FLACC for children who cannot self-report (2 months–7 years or nonverbal), FACES for 3 years and older, numeric scale for about 8 years and older.

stem: The nurse receives hand-off report on four clients on a medical-surgical unit. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 72-year-old client with COPD whose SpO2 is 89% on 2 L/min nasal cannula, which is the client's documented baseline.
options.why: An SpO2 of 88-92% is an expected target for many clients with chronic CO2 retention; a stable baseline finding can wait.

options.text: A 45-year-old client with type 2 diabetes whose fasting blood glucose is 182 mg/dL.
options.why: Hyperglycemia at this level needs follow-up but is not an immediate threat to airway, breathing, or circulation.

options.text: A 66-year-old client 1 day after total hip arthroplasty who reports sudden shortness of breath and sharp chest pain.
options.why: Sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain after orthopedic surgery suggest pulmonary embolism, an acute, life-threatening breathing and circulation problem that needs immediate assessment.

options.text: A 58-year-old client with heart failure who is stable and waiting for discharge teaching.
options.why: A stable client awaiting teaching is the lowest priority; teaching can be done after unstable clients are assessed.

takeaway: New, sudden changes that threaten breathing or circulation come before expected findings of chronic, stable conditions.

stem: Which task can the RN delegate to unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?

options.text: Teaching a client with newly diagnosed diabetes how to self-inject insulin.
options.why: Teaching requires nursing judgment and is an RN responsibility; it cannot be delegated to UAP.

options.text: Assessing a client's pain level 30 minutes after an IV opioid dose.
options.why: Evaluating the response to a medication is assessment, which belongs to the licensed nurse.

options.text: Ambulating a client for the first time after abdominal surgery.
options.why: The first ambulation after surgery requires the RN to assess tolerance, orthostatic changes, and safety; later routine ambulation of a stable client can be delegated.

options.text: Measuring and recording vital signs for a stable client 2 days after surgery.
options.why: Routine vital signs on a stable client are a standard, predictable task within UAP scope; the RN interprets the results.

takeaway: UAP may perform routine, predictable tasks on stable clients; assessment, teaching, evaluation, and judgment stay with the RN.

stem: The RN is making assignments with a licensed practical nurse (LPN). Which client is most appropriate to assign to the LPN?

options.text: A client with a stable chronic leg ulcer who needs a sterile dressing change and scheduled oral medications.
options.why: The client is stable with predictable needs, and sterile dressing changes and oral medications are within LPN scope.

options.text: A client admitted 1 hour ago with chest pain who needs an admission assessment.
options.why: The initial admission assessment of a client is an RN responsibility, and new chest pain makes this client potentially unstable.

options.text: A client with a new prescription for warfarin who needs discharge teaching.
options.why: Initial teaching is an RN responsibility; the LPN may reinforce teaching the RN has already provided.

options.text: A client 2 hours after cardiac catheterization whose blood pressure has dropped from 132/80 to 98/60 mmHg.
options.why: A falling blood pressure after an invasive procedure suggests bleeding; an unstable client needs RN assessment.

takeaway: Assign LPNs stable clients with predictable outcomes; keep new admissions, initial teaching, and unstable clients with the RN.

stem: At a mass casualty scene, the nurse uses START triage. An adult victim cannot walk and has a respiratory rate of 34/min. Which triage category should the nurse assign?

options.text: Minor (green)
options.why: Green is for the walking wounded; this victim cannot walk.

options.text: Immediate (red)
options.why: In START, a respiratory rate above 30/min indicates respiratory compromise and places the victim in the immediate (red) category.

options.text: Delayed (yellow)
options.why: Yellow requires a respiratory rate of 30/min or less, adequate perfusion, and the ability to follow commands; this victim's rate is above 30.

options.text: Expectant or deceased (black)
options.why: Black is used only when the victim does not breathe even after the airway is repositioned.

takeaway: START: walking = green; no breathing after airway opened = black; RR over 30, no radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds, or cannot follow commands = red; otherwise yellow.

stem: An emergency department nurse uses the Emergency Severity Index (ESI) for triage. Which client should be assigned ESI level 2?

options.text: A client in cardiac arrest who arrives with paramedics performing CPR.
options.why: A client who needs immediate lifesaving intervention is ESI level 1, not level 2.

options.text: A client with a swollen ankle after a twisting injury who can bear weight and needs an x-ray.
options.why: A stable client who needs one resource (an x-ray) is ESI level 4.

options.text: A 60-year-old client with chest pressure and diaphoresis whose vital signs are within normal limits.
options.why: Chest pressure with diaphoresis is a high-risk situation for acute coronary syndrome; a client who should not wait, even with normal vital signs, is ESI level 2.

options.text: A client requesting a refill of a blood pressure prescription.
options.why: A stable client who needs no resources is ESI level 5.

takeaway: ESI 1 needs immediate lifesaving intervention; ESI 2 is a high-risk situation, new confusion or lethargy, or severe pain or distress; ESI 3-5 are sorted by expected resources.

stem: A provider prescribes digoxin 2.5 mg PO daily for an adult client with heart failure. The nurse calls the provider to question the dose, and the provider refuses to change the prescription. What is the nurse's next action?

options.text: Administer the dose because the provider has confirmed the prescription.
options.why: The nurse is legally accountable for every medication given; a dose 10 to 20 times the usual adult dose (0.125-0.25 mg) is unsafe even if the provider confirms it.

options.text: Administer 0.25 mg, the usual dose, and document the reason.
options.why: Changing a dose without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope of practice.

options.text: Document the disagreement with the provider in the client's medical record.
options.why: The medical record is not the place to record interpersonal conflict, and documenting does not protect the client.

options.text: Withhold the medication and notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor.
options.why: When a provider will not change an unsafe prescription, the nurse withholds the drug and follows the chain of command to protect the client.

takeaway: Never give a medication you believe is unsafe; withhold it and go up the chain of command.

stem: The nurse finds a client sitting on the floor beside the bed. The client says, "I slipped trying to get to the bathroom." After assessing the client and notifying the provider, which documentation action is correct?

options.text: Complete an incident report with objective facts, and document the assessment in the medical record without mentioning the incident report.
options.why: The incident report is a confidential quality-improvement tool; the chart contains the factual assessment and care but no reference to the report.

options.text: Write "incident report completed" in the client's progress notes.
options.why: Referencing the incident report in the chart can make it part of the legal record and discoverable; it should not be mentioned.

options.text: Place a copy of the incident report in the client's medical record.
options.why: Incident reports are kept separate from the medical record and are filed according to facility policy.

options.text: Record in the incident report that the client fell because the UAP did not answer the call light.
options.why: Incident reports contain objective facts (for example, "client found sitting on floor" and the client's own words), not opinions or blame.

takeaway: Incident reports: objective facts only, no blame, never placed in or mentioned in the client's chart.

stem: The nurse brings a surgical consent form to a client scheduled for a mastectomy. The client says, "I'm not sure whether the surgeon is going to remove my lymph nodes too." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain the lymph node procedure to the client and then witness the signature.
options.why: Explaining the procedure, risks, benefits, and alternatives is the surgeon's responsibility, not the nurse's.

options.text: Have the client sign the form because the operating room is ready.
options.why: Consent signed without understanding is not informed consent; schedule pressure does not change that.

options.text: Hold the consent form and notify the surgeon that the client needs more information.
options.why: The nurse's role is to confirm understanding and witness the signature; when the client is not fully informed, the nurse stops and notifies the surgeon.

options.text: Ask the client's spouse to sign the consent on the client's behalf.
options.why: A competent adult client signs their own consent; a spouse cannot sign for a client who has decision-making capacity.

takeaway: The provider obtains informed consent; the nurse witnesses the signature and notifies the provider if the client does not understand.

stem: The charge nurse hears two UAPs arguing loudly in the hallway about who should care for a client who needs total assistance. What is the charge nurse's best initial action?

options.text: Tell both UAPs to stop and assign the client to the one with fewer clients.
options.why: An authoritarian decision ends the argument but does not address the cause and may leave lasting conflict.

options.text: Ask both UAPs to move to a private area and discuss the issue with each of them.
options.why: Moving the conflict out of public view protects clients and privacy, and hearing both sides allows a collaborative (win-win) solution.

options.text: Report both UAPs to the nurse manager for unprofessional behavior.
options.why: Escalating before trying to resolve the conflict at the unit level skips an appropriate first step.

options.text: Ignore the disagreement so the UAPs can work it out themselves.
options.why: Avoidance leaves the conflict unresolved and allows it to affect client care.

takeaway: Address staff conflict early, privately, and collaboratively; avoidance and authoritarian decisions rarely solve the root problem.

stem: Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with type 1 diabetes who is newly confused, diaphoretic, and shaky.
options.why: New confusion with diaphoresis and tremors suggests acute hypoglycemia, which can rapidly cause seizures and brain injury; this acute, unexpected change is the priority.

options.text: A client with Alzheimer's disease who is oriented to person only, which is documented as the client's baseline.
options.why: Disorientation that matches a documented baseline is an expected chronic finding.

options.text: A client with chronic kidney disease whose potassium is 5.3 mEq/L and who is scheduled for dialysis this morning.
options.why: A mildly elevated potassium is expected in chronic kidney disease, and treatment (dialysis) is already planned.

options.text: A client with rheumatoid arthritis who reports 60 minutes of morning joint stiffness.
options.why: Morning stiffness is an expected finding of rheumatoid arthritis and is not life-threatening.

takeaway: Acute and unexpected beats chronic and expected, even when the chronic client's numbers look abnormal.

stem: A client with a new tracheostomy has four needs. Which should the nurse address first?

options.text: Anxiety about being unable to speak.
options.why: Psychosocial needs matter but come after physiological needs such as a patent airway.

options.text: Incision pain rated 4 out of 10.
options.why: Pain is a physiological need, but moderate pain is not as urgent as a threatened airway.

options.text: Worry about how the tracheostomy will look to others.
options.why: Body image is a self-esteem need, which is lower priority on Maslow's hierarchy.

options.text: Coarse, gurgling respirations with SpO2 decreasing from 96% to 90%.
options.why: Gurgling respirations and falling oxygen saturation indicate secretions blocking the airway; airway is the first priority, and the nurse should suction.

takeaway: Use Maslow and ABCs: airway problems come before pain, safety, and psychosocial needs.

stem: An RN from the surgical unit is floated to a medical-cardiac unit for the shift. Which client should the charge nurse assign to the float nurse?

options.text: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis receiving an insulin infusion that requires hourly titration.
options.why: A complex, titrated, high-alert infusion is better assigned to a nurse familiar with the unit's protocols.

options.text: A client with cellulitis of the leg receiving IV antibiotics every 8 hours.
options.why: A stable client with care needs similar to those on a surgical unit (IV antibiotics, wound and skin assessment) is the best match for a float nurse.

options.text: A client with new-onset atrial fibrillation receiving a diltiazem infusion titrated to heart rate.
options.why: Titrating a cardiac drip on telemetry requires specialty experience the float nurse may not have.

options.text: A client with unstable angina who has new chest pain and is scheduled for cardiac catheterization in 1 hour.
options.why: An unstable cardiac client should be cared for by an experienced unit nurse.

takeaway: Assign float staff stable clients whose care resembles their usual practice; keep unstable or specialty-protocol clients with unit staff.

stem: A UAP reports the following data. Which finding requires the RN's immediate follow-up?

options.text: A temperature of 37.6 °C (99.7 °F) in a client 1 day after surgery.
options.why: A low-grade temperature is common in the first 24-48 hours after surgery and is not an emergency.

options.text: Urine output of 240 mL over the past 8 hours.
options.why: 240 mL over 8 hours is 30 mL/hr, which meets the usual minimum for adequate urine output.

options.text: Blood pressure 86/50 mmHg and heart rate 122/min in a client whose earlier blood pressure was 128/76 mmHg.
options.why: Hypotension with tachycardia is an acute change suggesting bleeding or shock; the RN must assess the client immediately.

options.text: A client ate 50% of breakfast.
options.why: Reduced appetite should be noted but is not urgent.

takeaway: The RN must personally follow up on any UAP report that suggests instability, such as new hypotension with tachycardia.

stem: A hospital activates its disaster plan and asks nurses to identify clients who can be discharged to make room for incoming casualties. Which client is most appropriate to discharge?

options.text: A client 6 hours after an open bowel resection.
options.why: A client in the immediate postoperative period after major surgery needs ongoing monitoring for bleeding and complications.

options.text: A client with an upper gastrointestinal bleed whose hemoglobin is 7.6 g/dL and who is awaiting a blood transfusion.
options.why: Active bleeding with significant anemia requiring transfusion makes this client unstable.

options.text: A client with a COPD exacerbation who intermittently requires BiPAP.
options.why: A client who still needs noninvasive ventilation has an ongoing breathing problem and is not ready for discharge.

options.text: A client with pneumonia who has been afebrile for 48 hours, has an SpO2 of 95% on room air, and now takes oral antibiotics.
options.why: This client is stable, improving, oxygenating on room air, and on oral therapy, so care can safely continue at home.

takeaway: In a disaster, discharge stable, improving clients whose remaining care can be given at home or as outpatients.

stem: Which activity must the RN perform and NOT assign to a licensed practical nurse (LPN)?

options.text: Performing the initial assessment of a newly admitted client.
options.why: Initial assessment and the nursing care plan are RN responsibilities; the LPN may collect data and contribute to ongoing assessment.

options.text: Administering a scheduled oral antihypertensive to a stable client.
options.why: Giving oral medications to stable clients is within LPN scope of practice.

options.text: Reinforcing discharge teaching that the RN has already provided.
options.why: LPNs may reinforce teaching; they may not provide the initial teaching.

options.text: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter in a stable client.
options.why: Sterile procedures such as urinary catheter insertion are within LPN scope.

takeaway: RN-only: initial assessment, care planning, initial teaching, evaluation, and care of unstable clients.

stem: After performing hand hygiene, which sequence should the nurse use to put on personal protective equipment (PPE) before entering a client's room?

options.text: Gloves, gown, mask, goggles
options.why: Putting gloves on first prevents the glove cuffs from covering the gown cuffs and risks contaminating the gloves while putting on other items.

options.text: Gown, mask, goggles, gloves
options.why: CDC donning order is gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, then gloves pulled over the gown cuffs.

options.text: Mask, gloves, gown, goggles
options.why: Gloves must go on last so they cover the gown cuffs and stay clean.

options.text: Goggles, mask, gloves, gown
options.why: Putting the gown on last means it is tied over the gloves and other equipment, which is incorrect.

takeaway: Donning: gown, mask/respirator, goggles/face shield, gloves (gloves last).

stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. The nurse is wearing a gown, gloves, a face shield, and a surgical mask. Which removal sequence is correct?

options.text: Mask, face shield, gown, gloves
options.why: Removing the mask first while still wearing contaminated gloves risks contaminating the face and mucous membranes.

options.text: Gown, mask, gloves, face shield
options.why: The gloves are the most contaminated item and should come off first (or together with the gown), and the mask should come off last.

options.text: Face shield, mask, gloves, gown
options.why: Touching the face shield and mask with contaminated gloves risks exposure of the face.

options.text: Gloves, face shield, gown, mask, then hand hygiene
options.why: CDC doffing order removes the most contaminated items first: gloves, face shield or goggles, gown, then mask, followed by hand hygiene.

takeaway: Doffing: gloves, goggles/face shield, gown, mask/respirator, then hand hygiene (mask last; remove a respirator after leaving the room).

stem: After caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) infection, which hand hygiene method should the nurse use?

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rub, rubbing until the hands are dry.
options.why: Alcohol does not reliably kill C. diff spores.

options.text: Rinsing the hands under running water without soap.
options.why: Water alone does not remove spores and organisms effectively.

options.text: Washing with soap and water, using friction.
options.why: The mechanical friction and rinsing of soap-and-water handwashing physically remove C. diff spores, which alcohol does not kill.

options.text: Alcohol-based hand rub followed immediately by a new pair of gloves.
options.why: Gloves over hands that still carry spores do not solve the problem; soap and water are required.

takeaway: C. diff: contact precautions, soap-and-water handwashing, and bleach-based (sporicidal) cleaning.

stem: A client with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is in an airborne infection isolation room and must be transported to radiology. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Place a surgical mask on the client for transport.
options.why: A surgical mask on the client contains respiratory droplets at the source; clients may leave the room for essential tests when masked.

options.text: Place a fit-tested N95 respirator on the client for transport.
options.why: N95 respirators protect staff from inhaling droplet nuclei; for source control the client wears a surgical mask.

options.text: Postpone the test until the client has three negative sputum smears.
options.why: Necessary diagnostic tests should not be delayed; a masked client can be transported safely.

options.text: Have the transporter wear a surgical mask while the client remains unmasked.
options.why: A surgical mask does not protect the wearer from airborne droplet nuclei, and an unmasked client spreads organisms along the route.

takeaway: Airborne (TB): negative-pressure room, fit-tested N95 for staff, surgical mask on the client when outside the room.

stem: A client is admitted with fever, nuchal rigidity, and a petechial rash. Bacterial meningitis is suspected, and IV antibiotics have been started. Which precautions should the nurse implement?

options.text: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room.
options.why: Meningococcal disease spreads by large respiratory droplets, not airborne droplet nuclei, so a negative-pressure room is not required.

options.text: Droplet precautions in a private room until 24 hours after effective antibiotic therapy begins.
options.why: Neisseria meningitidis spreads by droplets; a private room and a surgical mask for staff are needed until 24 hours of effective therapy.

options.text: Contact precautions only.
options.why: Contact precautions do not protect against respiratory droplets.

options.text: Standard precautions only, because antibiotics have already been started.
options.why: The client remains infectious until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy have been completed.

takeaway: Meningococcal meningitis: droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

stem: An 80-year-old client at high risk for falls becomes confused at night. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Raise all four side rails.
options.why: Four raised side rails count as a restraint, and confused clients who climb over them fall from a greater height.

options.text: Apply a vest restraint during the night.
options.why: Restraints are a last resort, require a prescription, and can increase injury and agitation.

options.text: Give a sedative-hypnotic at bedtime.
options.why: Sedatives increase confusion and fall risk in older adults.

options.text: Keep the bed low and locked, the call light in reach, and round hourly.
options.why: These are least-restrictive, evidence-based fall prevention measures.

takeaway: Fall prevention: low, locked bed, call light in reach, scheduled rounding and toileting; avoid four side rails and sedatives.

stem: A client has bilateral soft wrist restraints to prevent removal of an endotracheal tube. Which finding reported by the UAP requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: The fingers of the right hand are pale and cool, with capillary refill of 4 seconds.
options.why: Pale, cool fingers with delayed capillary refill indicate impaired circulation; the nurse must assess and loosen or reapply the restraint right away.

options.text: The restraints are tied to the bed frame with quick-release knots.
options.why: Securing to the bed frame (not the side rail) with a quick-release knot is correct practice.

options.text: Two fingers fit between each restraint and the client's wrist.
options.why: A two-finger fit is the correct tightness.

options.text: Skin checks and range of motion were done on each wrist 1 hour ago.
options.why: Releasing each limb for skin checks, range of motion, and toileting at least every 2 hours is correct; this was done on time.

takeaway: Monitor restrained limbs for circulation, sensation, and skin; tie to the bed frame with a quick-release knot, never to the side rail.

stem: The nurse discovers smoke and flames in a client's room. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Activate the fire alarm.
options.why: Alarm is the second step of RACE, after rescuing anyone in immediate danger.

options.text: Close the doors to the room and the corridor.
options.why: Containing the fire is the third step of RACE.

options.text: Remove the client from immediate danger.
options.why: RACE begins with Rescue: move clients in immediate danger away from the fire first.

options.text: Use a fire extinguisher on the flames.
options.why: Extinguishing (using PASS) is the last step and only if the fire is small and safe to fight.

takeaway: RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish; extinguisher use is PASS: Pull, Aim at the base, Squeeze, Sweep.

stem: While the nurse is giving morning medications, the client says, "That white pill is not the one I usually take." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that generic medications often look different and give the pill.
options.why: This may be true, but giving the drug without checking ignores a possible medication error.

options.text: Withhold the pill and verify it against the prescription and with the pharmacy.
options.why: A client's concern about a medication should always be investigated before administration to make sure the right drug and dose are being given.

options.text: Give the other medications and document that the client refused the white pill.
options.why: The client raised a question rather than refusing, and the possible error still needs investigation.

options.text: Ask the client to take the pill now and tell the provider about the concern later.
options.why: Giving a medication that may be wrong and checking later puts the client at risk.

takeaway: When a client questions a medication, stop and verify before giving it.

stem: Before giving a medication, which action best verifies the client's identity?

options.text: Check the room and bed number against the medication administration record.
options.why: Room and bed numbers are never acceptable identifiers because clients move and can be in the wrong bed.

options.text: Call out the client's name and wait for a response.
options.why: A confused, drowsy, or hard-of-hearing client may answer to any name.

options.text: Rely on recognizing the client from earlier in the shift.
options.why: Recognition is not a verified identifier and can lead to errors with similar-looking clients.

options.text: Ask the client to state their name and date of birth, and compare them with the ID band.
options.why: Two client-specific identifiers stated by the client and matched to the band and record meet patient safety standards.

takeaway: Use two identifiers (such as name and date of birth), never the room number, and have the client state them.

stem: Fifteen minutes after a unit of packed red blood cells is started, the client reports chills and low back pain. Temperature has risen from 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) to 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), and blood pressure has dropped from 124/76 to 92/58 mmHg. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Notify the provider and the blood bank.
options.why: Notification is required but comes after the transfusion is stopped to limit further exposure.

options.text: Obtain blood and urine samples for laboratory testing.
options.why: Samples are collected per protocol after the transfusion is stopped and the client is stabilized.

options.text: Stop the transfusion and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing.
options.why: These signs suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stopping the blood limits the amount of incompatible blood given, and new tubing keeps the IV access open without giving the blood left in the old tubing.

options.text: Slow the transfusion and give acetaminophen as prescribed.
options.why: Slowing the infusion continues to give incompatible blood, and acetaminophen does not treat a hemolytic reaction.

takeaway: For any suspected transfusion reaction, first stop the transfusion and keep the vein open with normal saline through new tubing.

stem: The nurse sets up a sterile field for a dressing change. Which event requires the nurse to discard the field and set up a new one?

options.text: The nurse left the room briefly to get a forgotten supply, leaving the field unattended.
options.why: A sterile field that is out of the nurse's sight is considered contaminated, because sterility cannot be confirmed.

options.text: The nurse dropped sterile gauze onto the center of the field from about 15 cm (6 inches) above it.
options.why: Dropping sterile items onto the field without touching it is the correct technique.

options.text: The nurse opened the first flap of the sterile package away from the body.
options.why: Opening the first flap away from the body is correct and avoids reaching over the field.

options.text: The nurse poured sterile saline into a sterile basin with the label facing the palm.
options.why: Pouring with the label against the palm protects the label and does not contaminate the field.

takeaway: A sterile field must stay in view; unattended, below waist level, wet-through, or touched by nonsterile items means contaminated.

stem: Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care to prevent pressure injury in an immobile client?

options.text: Massage reddened areas over bony prominences.
options.why: Massaging reddened skin can damage fragile tissue and is not recommended.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower and reposition at least every 2 hours.
options.why: A low head-of-bed angle reduces shear and sliding, and regular repositioning relieves pressure on bony prominences.

options.text: Use a ring (donut) cushion when the client sits in a chair.
options.why: Ring cushions concentrate pressure on surrounding tissue and reduce circulation.

options.text: Place several layers of linen and underpads under the client to absorb moisture.
options.why: Extra layers trap heat and moisture and reduce the effect of pressure-redistributing surfaces; use a single breathable pad and manage moisture directly.

takeaway: Prevent pressure injury with regular repositioning, head of bed 30 degrees or lower, pressure-redistributing surfaces, and no massage of red skin.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who will use oxygen at home. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will put 'No Smoking' signs in my home."
options.why: This is correct; smoking near oxygen is a major fire risk.

options.text: "I will keep my oxygen at least 10 feet away from the gas stove and candles."
options.why: This is correct; oxygen should be kept well away from open flames and heat sources.

options.text: "I will put petroleum jelly in my nose when it feels dry."
options.why: Petroleum-based products are flammable in an oxygen-rich environment; the client should use a water-based lubricant.

options.text: "I will store my extra oxygen tanks upright and secured."
options.why: This is correct; securing tanks prevents them from falling and being damaged.

takeaway: Home oxygen: no smoking or open flames nearby, water-based lubricants only, secure tanks upright.

stem: Which action by the nurse demonstrates correct body mechanics when moving a client or equipment?

options.text: Keeping a wide base of support and holding the load close to the body.
options.why: A wide base of support improves stability, and keeping the load close reduces strain on the back.

options.text: Bending at the waist with the knees straight to lift.
options.why: Bending at the waist strains the lower back; the nurse should bend at the hips and knees.

options.text: Twisting at the trunk to turn while carrying the load.
options.why: Twisting while lifting is a common cause of back injury; the nurse should pivot the feet instead.

options.text: Lifting a dependent adult client alone when no lift device is nearby.
options.why: Safe patient handling requires lift devices or additional staff for dependent clients.

takeaway: Body mechanics: wide base, load close, bend knees not waist, pivot don't twist, and use lift devices for dependent clients.

stem: A client receives NPH (intermediate-acting) insulin subcutaneously at 0700. During which time period is the client at greatest risk for hypoglycemia?

options.why: This matches the onset of rapid-acting insulin (about 15 minutes), not NPH.
NPH begins to act only 1 to 2 hours after injection, so peak risk is not this early.
NPH peaks about 4 to 12 hours after injection, so the greatest risk is from late morning through the afternoon; an afternoon snack helps prevent hypoglycemia.

options.text: 0700 the next morning
options.why: NPH lasts about 12 to 18 hours, so its effect is mostly gone by the next morning.

takeaway: Know insulin peaks: rapid-acting 1-3 hours, regular 2-4 hours, NPH 4-12 hours; glargine has no pronounced peak.

stem: A client is receiving a continuous IV heparin infusion. The aPTT result is 118 seconds (therapeutic range per protocol: 60-85 seconds), and the client has pink-tinged urine. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Stop the heparin infusion and notify the provider.
options.why: The aPTT is well above the therapeutic range and the client shows signs of bleeding; stopping the infusion is the priority, and the nurse should anticipate protamine sulfate if bleeding is significant.

options.text: Prepare to give vitamin K (phytonadione).
options.why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; the heparin antidote is protamine sulfate.

options.text: Decrease the infusion rate by 2 mL/hr and recheck the aPTT in 6 hours.
options.why: A small rate reduction is not appropriate when the aPTT is markedly high and the client is actively bleeding.

options.text: Continue the infusion and send a urine sample for urinalysis.
options.why: Continuing heparin with active bleeding and a supratherapeutic aPTT puts the client at risk of serious hemorrhage.

takeaway: Heparin: monitor aPTT (or anti-Xa); for bleeding with a high value, stop the infusion, notify the provider, and anticipate protamine sulfate.

stem: A client with atrial fibrillation is being discharged on warfarin. Which statement by the client indicates correct understanding of the teaching?

options.text: "I can take ibuprofen for my arthritis pain."
options.why: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen increase the risk of bleeding with warfarin and should be avoided unless the provider approves.

options.text: "My INR goal is less than 1.0."
options.why: The usual INR goal for atrial fibrillation is 2.0 to 3.0; an INR near 1.0 means no anticoagulant effect.

options.text: "If I bleed too much, protamine sulfate will reverse my warfarin."
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin; warfarin is reversed with vitamin K (phytonadione), and with prothrombin complex concentrate for serious bleeding.

options.text: "I will keep the amount of leafy green vegetables I eat about the same each week."
options.why: Vitamin K in leafy greens affects warfarin; a consistent intake, not avoidance, keeps the INR stable.

takeaway: Warfarin: INR goal usually 2-3, consistent vitamin K intake, avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless prescribed, antidote is vitamin K.

stem: Before giving digoxin 0.125 mg PO, the nurse finds an apical pulse of 64/min and a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L. The client reports nausea and seeing yellow halos around lights. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the dose because the apical pulse is above 60/min.
options.why: A heart rate above 60 does not rule out toxicity; nausea and visual changes are classic signs of digoxin toxicity.

options.text: Withhold the dose and notify the provider.
options.why: Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity, and nausea with yellow visual halos suggests toxicity is already present; the nurse holds the dose and anticipates a digoxin level and potassium replacement.

options.text: Give the dose with a potassium-rich food such as a banana.
options.why: Food will not correct a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L quickly, and the toxicity signs mean the dose must be held.

options.text: Give the dose and recheck the apical pulse in 1 hour.
options.why: Giving another dose to a client with signs of toxicity could cause dangerous dysrhythmias.

takeaway: Hold digoxin for signs of toxicity (nausea, vomiting, visual changes, dysrhythmias), even if the pulse is above 60; low potassium raises the risk.

stem: Which potassium chloride prescription should the nurse question?

options.text: Potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL, infused over 1 hour by infusion pump through a peripheral IV.
options.why: 10 mEq/hr is a commonly accepted maximum rate through a peripheral line when given by pump.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq added to 1,000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride at 100 mL/hr.
options.why: This delivers 2 mEq/hr in a dilute solution, which is safe.

options.text: Potassium chloride 10 mEq IV push over 2 minutes.
options.why: IV potassium is never given by IV push; a rapid bolus can cause cardiac arrest.

options.text: Potassium chloride 20 mEq PO twice daily with meals.
options.why: Oral potassium with meals is appropriate and reduces gastrointestinal irritation.

takeaway: IV potassium: always diluted, on a pump, never IV push, and confirm adequate urine output first.

stem: Twenty minutes into an IV vancomycin infusion, the client develops flushing and an itchy red rash on the face, neck, and upper chest. Blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, and there is no wheezing or throat tightness. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give epinephrine intramuscularly.
options.why: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis; this client has no hypotension, wheezing, or airway swelling.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate so the dose finishes sooner.
options.why: This reaction is caused by infusing too fast; speeding up makes it worse.

options.text: Continue the infusion and apply cool compresses to the rash.
options.why: Continuing at the same rate allows the reaction to progress.

options.text: Stop the infusion and notify the provider.
options.why: These are signs of vancomycin infusion reaction (red man syndrome), a rate-related histamine release; stop the infusion, then expect to restart more slowly (over at least 60 minutes) with an antihistamine.

takeaway: Vancomycin: infuse over at least 60 minutes to prevent infusion reaction; monitor drug levels per protocol (AUC-guided dosing is now preferred; troughs are drawn just before the next dose), and monitor kidney function.

stem: A client receiving IV gentamicin reports ringing in the ears and dizziness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the next dose and notify the provider.
options.why: Tinnitus and dizziness are signs of aminoglycoside ototoxicity, which can become permanent; the nurse holds the dose and anticipates drug levels and kidney function tests.

options.text: Explain that these are expected effects and continue the medication.
options.why: Ototoxicity is a serious adverse effect, not an expected one.

options.text: Give the dose and request a prescription for meclizine.
options.why: Treating the dizziness hides a sign of toxicity while the drug keeps causing damage.

options.text: Encourage extra fluids and give the next dose as scheduled.
options.why: Hydration supports the kidneys but does not reverse ototoxicity; giving more drug increases the harm.

takeaway: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin): watch for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity; monitor levels, creatinine, and hearing.

stem: A client who had surgery today is using a morphine PCA pump. The client has a respiratory rate of 7/min, is difficult to arouse, and has an SpO2 of 86%. The nurse stops the PCA, stimulates the client, and supports ventilation. Which describes correct naloxone administration?

options.text: Give naloxone 2 mg rapid IV push to completely reverse the opioid.
options.why: Rapid full reversal can cause severe pain, withdrawal, hypertension, and dysrhythmias in a postoperative client.

options.text: Dilute naloxone 0.4 mg in 10 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride and give small increments slowly, titrating to respiratory rate and level of consciousness.
options.why: Titrating diluted naloxone reverses respiratory depression while keeping as much pain relief as possible.

options.text: Give one dose, then stop monitoring once the respiratory rate is above 12/min because naloxone lasts longer than morphine.
options.why: Naloxone has a shorter duration than morphine, so respiratory depression can return; continued close monitoring is required.

options.text: Wait until the respiratory rate falls below 4/min before giving naloxone.
options.why: The client is already hypoxic and difficult to arouse; waiting risks respiratory arrest.
