options.why: Correct. PAINAD scores observable behaviors such as breathing, vocalization, facial expression, body language, and consolability.

takeaway: Use a behavioral tool such as PAINAD for adults with advanced dementia who cannot self-report.

stem: A client who is actively dying has noisy, gurgling respirations. The family is upset by the sound. Which nursing action is best?

options.text: Perform deep nasotracheal suctioning every hour.
options.why: Deep suctioning is uncomfortable, often ineffective for these secretions, and can increase distress.

options.text: Place the client flat on the back.
options.why: Supine positioning lets secretions pool in the throat and makes the sound worse.

options.text: Increase the IV fluid rate.
options.why: Extra fluids can increase secretions and worsen the gurgling.

options.text: Turn the client onto the side with the head of the bed raised, and explain that the sound is not usually distressing to the client.
options.why: Correct. Side-lying and elevation help secretions drain; explaining the cause supports the family.

takeaway: For end-of-life noisy breathing, reposition side-lying with head raised and educate the family; avoid routine deep suctioning.

stem: A client in the final days of life refuses food and coughs when given liquids. The client's daughter insists on feeding full meals. Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "Keep encouraging her to finish each meal so she keeps her strength."
options.why: Forcing food causes discomfort and increases the risk of aspiration.

options.text: "Feeding her could harm her, so please stop."
options.why: This is true in part but dismissive; it does not explain or offer the daughter another way to help.

options.text: "Decreased hunger is a normal part of dying. You can offer small sips or ice chips if your mother wants them, and help with mouth care."
options.why: Correct. This educates the family, respects the client's wishes, and gives the daughter a meaningful way to provide comfort while reducing aspiration risk.

options.text: "I will ask the provider about placing a feeding tube."
options.why: Artificial nutrition at the end of life does not usually improve comfort or survival and is not the first response.

takeaway: At the end of life, offer food and fluids only for comfort, provide mouth care, and teach the family that loss of appetite is expected.

stem: The nurse is caring for a client who just had a plaster cast applied to the forearm. Which action is correct while the cast dries?

options.text: Rest the cast on a hard surface to keep its shape.
options.why: Hard surfaces can flatten the wet cast; it should rest on a pillow.

options.text: Handle the cast with the palms of the hands.
options.why: Correct. Palms spread pressure evenly; fingertips can make dents that press on the skin underneath.

options.text: Cover the cast with a blanket to keep the arm warm.
options.why: Covering traps heat and slows drying; the cast should be left open to air.

options.text: Use a heat lamp to speed drying.
options.why: External heat can burn the skin under the cast and causes uneven drying.

takeaway: Handle a wet plaster cast with palms only, support it on pillows, and leave it uncovered to dry.

stem: A client with a femur fracture is in balanced skeletal traction. The nurse finds that the traction weights are resting on the floor. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Reposition the client up toward the head of the bed so the weights hang freely.
options.why: Correct. The client has slid down; moving the client up restores the countertraction and free-hanging weights.

options.text: Shorten the rope by tying a knot near the pulley.
options.why: Knots can catch in the pulley and changing the rope alters the prescribed traction setup.

options.text: Lift the weights and set them on the bed frame.
options.why: Weights must hang freely to provide continuous pull.

options.text: Remove the weights until the client is repositioned.
options.why: Removing weights releases traction and can cause pain and fragment movement; weights stay on unless prescribed otherwise.

takeaway: Traction weights must hang freely at all times; reposition the client rather than moving the weights.

stem: A client who takes warfarin tells the nurse about several supplements the client uses. Which supplement is the nurse's greatest concern?

options.text: Ginkgo biloba
options.why: Correct. Ginkgo inhibits platelet function and can increase the risk of bleeding with warfarin.

options.text: Probiotic capsules
options.why: Probiotics are not known to have a significant interaction with warfarin.

options.text: Topical aloe vera gel
options.why: Topical aloe on the skin is not expected to affect anticoagulation.

options.text: Calcium carbonate
options.why: Calcium carbonate does not significantly affect warfarin's anticoagulant effect.

takeaway: Ginkgo, garlic, and ginseng can increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants; ask every client about supplements.

stem: The nurse is performing passive range-of-motion exercises for a client with left-sided hemiplegia. Which technique is correct?

options.text: Move each joint past the point of resistance to increase flexibility.
options.why: Forcing beyond resistance can injure joints, muscles, and ligaments.

options.text: Perform the exercises once a week.
options.why: Range of motion should be done at least two to three times daily to prevent contractures.

options.text: Support the limb above and below the joint and move it slowly to the point of resistance.
options.why: Correct. Supporting the limb and moving smoothly to resistance, not pain, protects the joint.

options.text: Perform fast repetitions so the exercise can be completed quickly.
options.why: Rapid movement can increase spasticity and cause injury; movements should be slow and smooth.

takeaway: Passive ROM: support the joint, move slowly and smoothly, and stop at resistance or pain.

stem: The nurse is reviewing care for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which actions help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder.
options.why: Correct. This prevents backflow of urine into the bladder.

options.text: Secure the catheter to the client's upper thigh.
options.why: Correct. Securing the catheter prevents movement and urethral trauma.

options.text: Clean the urinary meatus with soap and water during daily hygiene.
options.why: Correct. Routine hygiene is recommended; antiseptic cleaning is not needed.

options.text: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing to collect a urine specimen.
options.why: Breaking the closed system lets bacteria enter; specimens are taken from the sampling port.

options.text: Irrigate the catheter daily to keep it open.
options.why: Routine irrigation is not recommended and opens the closed system.

options.text: Rest the drainage bag on the floor so it drains well.
options.why: The bag must not touch the floor because of contamination risk.

takeaway: Prevent CAUTI: closed system, bag below bladder and off the floor, catheter secured, daily hygiene.

stem: The nurse is teaching foot care to a client with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect your feet every day, using a mirror for the soles.
options.why: Correct. Loss of sensation means injuries may go unnoticed; daily inspection finds them early.

options.text: Dry carefully between your toes after washing.
options.why: Correct. Moisture between the toes promotes fungal infection and skin breakdown.

options.text: Wear well-fitting shoes and socks, and do not walk barefoot.
options.why: Correct. This protects numb feet from injury.

options.text: Soak your feet in warm water for 20 minutes each day.
options.why: Soaking dries and macerates skin, and the client may not feel water that is too hot.

options.text: Apply lotion between your toes to prevent dryness.
options.why: Lotion between the toes keeps the area moist and promotes infection; apply it to the tops and soles only.

options.text: Cut off corns with a razor blade.
options.why: Self-treating corns can cause wounds and infection; a podiatrist should treat them.

takeaway: Diabetic foot care: inspect daily, keep feet clean and dry, wear shoes, no soaking or self-treating corns.

stem: A client is on bed rest after a stroke. Which interventions should the nurse include to prevent complications of immobility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours.
options.why: Correct. Regular turning relieves pressure on bony prominences.

options.text: Apply high-top sneakers or foot boots on a schedule.
options.why: Correct. Keeping the foot at 90 degrees prevents plantar flexion contracture (footdrop).

options.text: Encourage deep breathing and coughing every 1 to 2 hours while awake.
options.why: Correct. This helps prevent atelectasis and pneumonia.

options.text: Encourage fluid intake of 2 to 3 L daily unless restricted.
options.why: Correct. Fluids help prevent constipation, urinary stasis, and kidney stones.

options.text: Massage reddened areas over bony prominences.
options.why: Massaging reddened skin can damage underlying tissue and is not recommended.

options.text: Keep a pillow under the knees at all times.
options.why: Constant knee flexion promotes knee contractures and slows venous return.

takeaway: Immobility affects every system: turn, prevent footdrop, deep breathe, and hydrate; never massage reddened bony areas.

stem: A client receiving palliative care for advanced cancer has ongoing nausea. Which nonpharmacological measures should the nurse use? Select all that apply.

options.text: Offer small, frequent meals of bland, cool foods.
options.why: Correct. Small portions and cool foods with less odor are better tolerated.

options.text: Remove the meal tray cover outside the room and limit strong odors.
options.why: Correct. Strong smells can trigger nausea.

options.text: Provide oral care before meals.
options.why: Correct. A clean mouth reduces unpleasant tastes and improves appetite.

options.text: Have the client lie flat after eating.
options.why: Lying flat after meals can increase nausea and reflux; keep the head raised.

options.text: Encourage the client to eat three large meals each day.
options.why: Large meals stretch the stomach and worsen nausea.

takeaway: Non-drug nausea relief: small cool bland meals, limit odors, mouth care, and stay upright after eating.

stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is going home with a new fiberglass arm cast. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep your arm raised above heart level for the first 24 to 48 hours.
options.why: Correct. Elevation reduces swelling under the cast.

options.text: Use a hair dryer on the cool setting if the skin under the cast itches.
options.why: Correct. Cool air can relieve itching safely.

options.text: Call your provider for numbness, tingling, or pain that gets worse.
options.why: Correct. These can be signs of nerve or circulation problems such as compartment syndrome.

options.text: Slide a ruler under the cast to scratch an itch.
options.why: Objects inside the cast can break the skin and cause infection.

options.text: Sprinkle powder inside the cast to keep it dry.
options.why: Powder can clump and irritate the skin.

options.text: It is fine to let the cast get wet in the shower.
options.why: Standard cast padding holds moisture and can cause skin breakdown; the cast should be kept dry unless it has a waterproof liner.

takeaway: Cast care: elevate, keep it dry, nothing inside the cast, and report numbness, tingling, or increasing pain.

stem: Which interventions should the nurse use to promote sleep for a hospitalized client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cluster care at night to allow longer periods of uninterrupted sleep.
options.why: Correct. Grouping tasks lets the client complete full sleep cycles.

options.text: Dim the lights and reduce noise at night.
options.why: Correct. A dark, quiet environment supports sleep.

options.text: Support the client's usual bedtime routine, such as reading.
options.why: Correct. Familiar routines signal the body to prepare for sleep.

options.text: Offer a cup of coffee with the evening snack.
options.why: Caffeine is a stimulant and interferes with sleep.

options.text: Leave the television on all night for company.
options.why: Light and noise from a television disrupt sleep.

takeaway: Promote sleep by clustering care, limiting light and noise, and supporting the client's routines.

stem: A client with dysphagia after a stroke is prescribed thickened liquids. Which actions should the nurse include to prevent aspiration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Seat the client upright at 90 degrees for meals.
options.why: Correct. An upright position uses gravity to help food move into the esophagus.

options.text: Have the client tuck the chin down when swallowing.
options.why: Correct. Chin tuck helps protect the airway during swallowing.

options.text: Keep the client upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
options.why: Correct. This reduces the risk of reflux and aspiration after meals.

options.text: Give liquids at the thickness prescribed by the speech-language pathologist.
options.why: Correct. Thickened liquids move more slowly and are easier to control.

options.text: Offer liquids through a straw.
options.why: Straws make liquid flow faster and harder to control, which increases aspiration risk.

options.text: Encourage the client to wash down solid food with sips of thin water.
options.why: Mixing consistencies and thin liquids increases aspiration risk for clients with dysphagia.

takeaway: Dysphagia: sit upright, chin tuck, prescribed liquid thickness, no straws, and stay upright 30 minutes after meals.

stem: The nurse is providing oral care to an unconscious client. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Turn the client to the side with the head turned toward the nurse.
options.why: Correct. Side-lying lets fluid drain out of the mouth instead of into the airway.

options.text: Have suction equipment ready at the bedside.
options.why: Correct. Suction removes pooled fluid and reduces aspiration risk.

options.text: Use a soft toothbrush or swab moistened with a small amount of fluid.
options.why: Correct. Small amounts of fluid clean the mouth safely.

options.text: Place the client flat on the back during care.
options.why: Supine positioning allows fluid to flow into the airway.

options.text: Rinse the mouth with a large amount of mouthwash.
options.why: Large amounts of fluid increase aspiration risk.

options.text: Use lemon-glycerin swabs to moisten the mouth.
options.why: Lemon-glycerin dries the mucosa and can damage tooth enamel.

takeaway: Oral care for unconscious clients: side-lying, suction ready, small amounts of fluid.

stem: The nurse is giving a cleansing enema to an adult client. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Insert the lubricated tip 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in) toward the umbilicus while the client breathes out slowly.
options.why: This follows positioning and lubrication; exhaling relaxes the anal sphincter.

options.text: Verify the prescription, explain the procedure, and perform hand hygiene.
options.why: This comes first to confirm the order, gain cooperation, and begin infection control.

options.text: Lubricate the tip of the tubing just before inserting it.
options.why: Lubrication is done immediately before insertion, after the client is positioned, to ease entry and reduce trauma.

options.text: Raise the container 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 in) above the anus and let the solution flow in slowly.
options.why: Instillation is the last step after the tube is in place; slow flow reduces cramping.

options.text: Place a waterproof pad, help the client into the left side-lying (Sims) position with the right knee flexed, and put on clean gloves.
options.why: Left side-lying follows the natural curve of the sigmoid colon and rectum; gloves are put on once the client is positioned.

takeaway: Enema: verify and explain, left Sims position and gloves, lubricate, insert 7.5 to 10 cm, then instill slowly from 30 to 45 cm high.

stem: The nurse is changing a client's colostomy pouching system. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Measure the clean, dry stoma with a measuring guide.
options.why: Measuring after cleaning ensures an accurate size for the barrier opening.

options.text: Gently remove the old pouch, pushing the skin away from the barrier.
options.why: Removal comes first; pushing the skin away reduces trauma.

options.text: Apply the barrier and hold a hand over it for 30 to 60 seconds.
options.why: Body heat helps the adhesive seal, which is the final step.

options.text: Clean the skin around the stoma with warm water and pat it dry.
options.why: Clean, dry skin is needed before measuring and for a good seal.

options.text: Cut the barrier opening about 1.5 to 3 mm (1/16 to 1/8 in) larger than the stoma.
options.why: Done after measuring; a slightly larger opening protects the stoma without exposing much skin.

takeaway: Pouch change: remove, clean and dry, measure, cut to fit, apply and hold.

stem: The nurse is helping a client with right-sided weakness move from the bed to a chair. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Apply a gait belt and help the client stand while bracing the client's weak knee with the nurse's knee.
options.why: Standing comes after sitting and dangling; the gait belt gives a secure hold and bracing the weak knee prevents buckling.

options.text: Pivot the client on the stronger left leg toward the chair.
options.why: The client turns on the strong leg once standing.

options.text: Before getting the client up, place the chair at the client's left side at a 45-degree angle and lock the bed and chair wheels.
options.why: Setting up the equipment comes first; the chair goes on the strong side.

options.text: Have the client reach back for the armrests and lower slowly into the chair.
options.why: This is the last step, giving a controlled sit.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and help the client sit on the edge with feet flat on the floor.
options.why: Sitting and dangling first allows the client to adjust and reduces orthostatic dizziness.

takeaway: Transfer toward the strong side: set up and lock, sit and dangle, stand, pivot on the strong leg, sit.

stem: A client is scheduled for a CT scan with IV contrast this afternoon. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider before the scan?

options.text: The client takes metformin and has a serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL.
options.why: Creatinine is well above normal (about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL); contrast can worsen kidney injury, and metformin with poor kidney function raises the risk of lactic acidosis.

options.text: The client's BUN is 15 mg/dL.
options.why: This is within the normal range of 10–20 mg/dL and does not need to be reported.

options.text: The client's hemoglobin is 13.5 g/dL.
options.why: This is a normal hemoglobin and does not affect contrast safety.

options.text: The client says a previous contrast injection caused a brief warm, flushed feeling.
options.why: A warm, flushed feeling is an expected effect of IV contrast, not an allergic reaction.

takeaway: Before IV contrast, check kidney function and report elevated creatinine, especially in a client taking metformin.

stem: Two hours after a bronchoscopy with topical anesthetic spray to the throat, a client asks for a drink of water. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check for return of the gag and swallow reflexes.
options.why: The throat is numbed for the procedure; the client may not eat or drink until the gag reflex returns, to prevent aspiration.

options.text: Give a few ice chips to soothe the throat.
options.why: Ice chips are still oral intake and can be aspirated if the gag reflex has not returned.

options.text: Offer small sips of water through a straw.
options.why: Sips of water carry the same aspiration risk until the reflexes are confirmed.

options.text: Tell the client fluids are not allowed for 24 hours.
options.why: There is no 24-hour restriction; fluids are resumed once the gag reflex returns, usually in 1–2 hours.

takeaway: After bronchoscopy, keep the client NPO until the gag and swallow reflexes return.

stem: The nurse is preparing a client with ascites for a paracentesis. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask the client to empty the bladder.
options.why: An empty bladder lowers the risk of puncturing the bladder with the needle.

options.text: Obtain a baseline weight and abdominal girth.
options.why: Baseline measurements let the nurse judge how much fluid was removed and track the client's progress.

options.text: Position the client upright on the edge of the bed or in high Fowler's position.
options.why: Sitting up lets fluid pool in the lower abdomen, where the needle is inserted.

options.text: Keep the client NPO for 12 hours before the procedure.
options.why: Paracentesis uses local anesthesia; a long fast is not needed.

options.text: Place the client in the prone position.
options.why: Lying prone does not allow access to the abdomen and is not used for paracentesis.

options.text: Record baseline vital signs.
options.why: Removing a large amount of fluid can cause hypotension, so baseline vital signs are needed for comparison.

takeaway: Before paracentesis: void, weigh, measure girth, take vital signs, and sit the client upright.

stem: A client had a lumbar puncture 6 hours ago. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Mild headache that improves when lying flat
options.why: A headache that improves when lying flat is a common post-puncture headache and is managed with rest and fluids.

options.text: New numbness and weakness in both legs
options.why: New neurologic deficits in the legs may mean a spinal epidural hematoma compressing the cord, which is an emergency.

options.text: A small, dry dressing over the puncture site
options.why: A dry, intact dressing is an expected finding.

options.text: Mild soreness at the puncture site
options.why: Mild local soreness is expected after a needle is placed in the lower back.

takeaway: After a lumbar puncture, new leg numbness or weakness is an emergency; a positional headache is common.

stem: Three hours after a colonoscopy with removal of a polyp, which finding requires the nurse's immediate action?

options.text: Passing flatus with mild cramping
options.why: Air is put into the colon during the procedure; gas and mild cramping are expected.

options.text: Severe abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen, and a temperature of 101.3°F (38.5°C)
options.why: These are signs of bowel perforation and peritonitis, which need urgent surgical evaluation.

options.text: A small streak of blood on toilet tissue
options.why: A small amount of blood can be expected after a polyp is removed.

options.text: Drowsiness, but the client wakes easily when spoken to
options.why: Mild drowsiness from moderate sedation is expected while it wears off.

takeaway: After colonoscopy, severe pain, a rigid abdomen, and fever suggest perforation; report it at once.

stem: The nurse is caring for a client who just had a percutaneous liver biopsy. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: On the right side with a pillow under the lower ribs
options.why: Lying on the right side presses the liver against the chest wall and helps prevent bleeding from the biopsy site.

options.text: On the left side with the knees flexed
options.why: The left side does not apply pressure to the liver puncture site.

options.text: In high Fowler's position
options.why: Sitting upright does not compress the biopsy site and does not help prevent bleeding.

options.text: Prone with the head turned to the side
options.why: Prone positioning is not used and does not target the liver site.

takeaway: After a liver biopsy, place the client on the right side to apply pressure to the site.

stem: A client who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation has an INR of 4.6. The client has no signs of bleeding. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the next warfarin dose and notify the provider.
options.why: The usual target INR for atrial fibrillation is 2.0–3.0; a value of 4.6 raises bleeding risk, so the dose is held and the provider decides on the next step.

options.text: Give the warfarin dose as scheduled.
options.why: Giving more warfarin would raise the INR further and increase bleeding risk.

options.text: Give IV vitamin K right away.
options.why: Vitamin K requires a prescription and is usually not given IV for a high INR without bleeding.

options.text: Give protamine sulfate.
options.why: Protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.

takeaway: For an INR above the target range, hold warfarin and notify the provider.

stem: A client is receiving a continuous IV infusion of unfractionated heparin per a weight-based protocol. The goal aPTT is 60–80 seconds. The 6-hour aPTT result is 118 seconds, and the client has no bleeding. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Hold the infusion as directed by the protocol, then resume at a lower rate and notify the provider.
options.why: The aPTT is well above the goal; protocols direct a brief hold and a rate decrease to reduce bleeding risk.

options.text: Increase the infusion rate.
options.why: Increasing the rate would raise the aPTT even more and could cause bleeding.

options.text: Continue the current rate and recheck the aPTT in 24 hours.
options.why: The value is dangerously high and needs action now, not in 24 hours.

options.text: Give vitamin K as prescribed.
options.why: Vitamin K reverses warfarin; protamine sulfate is the antidote for heparin.

takeaway: An aPTT above the goal range on heparin means hold or reduce the infusion per protocol and notify the provider.

stem: A client is scheduled for elective surgery tomorrow. The nurse reviews the preoperative lab results. Which results should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
options.why: Low potassium (normal 3.5–5.0 mEq/L) raises the risk of dysrhythmias during anesthesia.

options.text: Sodium 139 mEq/L
options.why: This is within the normal range of 135–145 mEq/L.

options.text: Platelets 92,000/mm³
options.why: Platelets below the normal 150,000–400,000/mm³ increase the risk of surgical bleeding.

options.text: INR 1.0
options.why: An INR of about 1.0 is normal for a client not taking anticoagulants.

options.text: Serum creatinine 2.1 mg/dL
options.why: High creatinine (normal about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL) shows reduced kidney function, which affects drug clearance and fluid management.

options.text: Fasting blood glucose 94 mg/dL
options.why: This is within the normal fasting range of 70–99 mg/dL.

takeaway: Report abnormal electrolytes, platelets, and kidney function before surgery so they can be corrected.

stem: Four hours after abdominal surgery, a client using a morphine PCA pump is drowsy with a respiratory rate of 9/min. ABG results: pH 7.29, PaCO2 54 mm Hg, HCO3 24 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Respiratory acidosis
options.why: pH is low (below 7.35) and PaCO2 is high (above 45 mm Hg) from slow breathing, with a normal bicarbonate.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis
options.why: Metabolic acidosis would show a low bicarbonate (below 22 mEq/L); here it is normal.

options.text: Respiratory alkalosis
options.why: Respiratory alkalosis has a high pH and low PaCO2, the opposite of these results.

options.text: Compensated metabolic alkalosis
options.why: The pH is acidic and the bicarbonate is normal, so this is not metabolic alkalosis.

takeaway: Low pH with high PaCO2 is respiratory acidosis; opioid-induced slow breathing is a common cause after surgery.

stem: A client who takes digoxin 0.125 mg daily reports nausea and seeing yellow halos around lights. The serum digoxin level is 2.8 ng/mL and potassium is 3.2 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the digoxin and notify the provider.
options.why: The level is above the therapeutic range (about 0.5–2.0 ng/mL) and the client has signs of toxicity; low potassium makes toxicity worse.

options.text: Give the digoxin with food to reduce nausea.
options.why: Nausea here is a sign of toxicity; giving more digoxin is unsafe.

options.text: Give the digoxin with an oral potassium supplement.
options.why: The potassium needs correcting, but digoxin must still be held while the level is toxic.

options.text: Give an antiemetic and continue the digoxin.
options.why: Treating the nausea hides a toxicity symptom and does not lower the dangerous level.

takeaway: Hold digoxin for a level above the therapeutic range or signs of toxicity, and check potassium.

stem: A client with type 2 diabetes has an HbA1c of 8.9%. The client says, "My sugar was normal at the clinic this morning, so my diabetes is under control." Which response by the nurse is best?

options.text: "The A1C shows your average blood sugar over the past 2 to 3 months, and this result is above the usual goal of less than 7%."
options.why: HbA1c reflects glucose control over about 3 months; 8.9% shows poor control despite one normal reading.

options.text: "One normal reading this morning confirms that your diabetes is controlled."
options.why: A single glucose value shows only one moment and does not reflect long-term control.

options.text: "The A1C measures your blood sugar over the past 24 hours."
options.why: HbA1c reflects about 2–3 months of glucose, not 24 hours.

options.text: "You should fast before the next A1C so the result is more accurate."
options.why: Fasting is not required for an HbA1c test.

takeaway: HbA1c reflects average glucose over 2–3 months; a common goal for adults with diabetes is below 7%.

stem: A client has received IV gentamicin for 5 days. The serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.9 mg/dL, and urine output is decreasing. The next dose is due in 1 hour. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the provider of possible nephrotoxicity.
options.why: A rising creatinine and falling urine output suggest kidney injury from the aminoglycoside; the provider must review the dose before more is given.

options.text: Give the dose and increase oral fluids.
options.why: Giving more gentamicin can worsen kidney injury; fluids alone do not make it safe.

options.text: Give the dose and draw a trough level afterward.
options.why: A trough is drawn before a dose, and the signs of kidney injury need to be reported first.

options.text: Give the dose with IV furosemide to increase urine output.
options.why: Loop diuretics with aminoglycosides increase the risk of ototoxicity and do not protect the kidneys.

takeaway: Rising creatinine during aminoglycoside therapy means hold the next dose and notify the provider.

stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 18,000/mm³. Which planned action should the nurse question?

options.text: Give a soap-suds enema for constipation.
options.why: Enemas can injure the rectal lining and cause bleeding when platelets are very low; they should be avoided.

options.text: Provide a soft-bristled toothbrush.
options.why: A soft toothbrush lowers the risk of gum bleeding and is appropriate.

options.text: Have the client use an electric razor.
options.why: An electric razor lowers the risk of cuts and is appropriate.

options.text: Give a stool softener daily.
options.why: A stool softener prevents straining and rectal injury, which is appropriate.

takeaway: With severe thrombocytopenia, avoid rectal procedures, injections, and anything that can cause tissue injury.

stem: A client with dysphagia after a stroke is starting a mechanical soft diet with thickened liquids. Which actions help reduce the risk of aspiration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Seat the client fully upright for meals.
options.why: An upright position helps food move down the esophagus and protects the airway.

options.text: Teach the client to tuck the chin when swallowing.
options.why: A chin tuck narrows the airway entrance and helps protect against aspiration.

options.text: Offer thin liquids through a straw.
options.why: Thin liquids and straws move fluid quickly and increase aspiration risk.

options.text: Keep the client upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
options.why: Staying upright after meals lowers the risk of reflux and aspiration.

options.text: Place food on the unaffected side of the mouth.
options.why: The unaffected side has better sensation and muscle control for chewing and swallowing.

options.text: Encourage the client to talk during meals to stay engaged.
options.why: Talking while eating opens the airway and increases aspiration risk.

takeaway: For dysphagia: sit upright, chin tuck, unaffected side, thickened liquids, no straws, and no talking while eating.

stem: A client is 1 day post open abdominal surgery. Which measures should the nurse use to help prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply sequential compression devices while the client is in bed.
options.why: Intermittent compression pushes blood out of the leg veins and reduces stasis.

options.text: Teach ankle pumps and leg exercises every hour while awake.
options.why: Muscle contraction in the calves promotes venous return.

options.text: Place a pillow under the client's knees.
options.why: Pressure behind the knees restricts venous flow and increases DVT risk.

options.text: Help the client ambulate early as prescribed.
options.why: Early walking is one of the most effective ways to prevent venous stasis.

options.text: Give subcutaneous enoxaparin as prescribed.
options.why: Low-molecular-weight heparin is a standard drug for DVT prevention after surgery.

options.text: Massage the calves to improve circulation.
options.why: Massaging the legs is avoided because it could dislodge an existing clot.

takeaway: Prevent post-op DVT with early ambulation, leg exercises, compression devices, and prescribed anticoagulants; never massage the calves.

stem: On the first day after upper abdominal surgery, a client has a temperature of 100.2°F (37.9°C), diminished breath sounds in both lung bases, and SpO2 of 93% on room air. The client is splinting the incision and taking shallow breaths. Which action is best?

options.text: Give the prescribed pain medication and coach the client to use the incentive spirometer 10 times per hour while awake.
options.why: These findings suggest atelectasis; pain control allows deep breaths, and incentive spirometry re-expands the alveoli.

options.text: Give acetaminophen and recheck the temperature in 4 hours.
options.why: This treats the fever but not the cause, which is collapsed alveoli from shallow breathing.

options.text: Keep the client on bed rest to conserve energy.
options.why: Immobility makes atelectasis worse; the client should be moving and ambulating.

options.text: Obtain blood cultures.
options.why: A low-grade fever in the first 1–2 days after surgery is most often from atelectasis, not a bloodstream infection.

takeaway: Early post-op low-grade fever with diminished bases suggests atelectasis: control pain and use the incentive spirometer.

stem: On the fifth day after abdominal surgery, a client coughs and says, "Something just gave way." The nurse sees loops of bowel through the opened incision. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Cover the wound with sterile dressings moistened with sterile normal saline.
options.why: Moist sterile coverage protects the exposed bowel from drying and contamination while help is called.

options.text: Gently push the bowel back into the abdomen.
options.why: Trying to replace the organs can cause injury and infection; only the surgeon does this in the OR.

options.text: Cover the wound with dry sterile gauze.
options.why: Dry gauze sticks to and dries out the bowel tissue.

options.text: Place the client flat in the supine position with the legs straight.
options.why: Flat with straight legs increases tension on the abdomen; low Fowler's with knees bent is preferred.

takeaway: For evisceration, cover the organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings, stay with the client, and call the surgeon.

stem: Two days after a bowel resection, a client has abdominal distention, nausea, hypoactive bowel sounds, and has not passed flatus. The client asks for something to eat. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep the client NPO and notify the provider; anticipate a nasogastric tube to low intermittent suction.
options.why: These are signs of paralytic ileus; feeding would worsen distention and vomiting, and the stomach may need to be decompressed.

options.text: Give clear liquids to stimulate the bowel.
options.why: Oral intake with an ileus increases distention and the risk of vomiting and aspiration.

options.text: Give a tap-water enema.
options.why: An enema needs a prescription and is unsafe soon after bowel surgery because it can stress the anastomosis.

options.text: Encourage the client to stay in bed to rest the bowel.
options.why: Ambulation helps restore peristalsis; bed rest slows recovery.

takeaway: Post-op distention, nausea, no flatus, and absent or hypoactive bowel sounds suggest ileus: keep NPO and notify the provider.

stem: Eight hours after an inguinal hernia repair under spinal anesthesia, a client has not voided and reports lower abdominal discomfort. The nurse palpates the bladder above the symphysis pubis. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Perform a bladder scan to measure the urine volume.
options.why: A bladder scan confirms retention and the volume, which guides whether catheterization is needed.

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter.
options.why: An indwelling catheter needs a prescription and is not the first step; straight catheterization is usually tried first after the volume is known.

options.text: Restrict oral fluids until the client voids.
options.why: Restricting fluids does not relieve retention and may cause dehydration.

options.text: Document the finding and reassess in 4 hours.
options.why: A distended, uncomfortable bladder needs action now; waiting risks bladder overdistention.

takeaway: Suspected post-op urinary retention: assess with a bladder scan before deciding on catheterization.

stem: The nurse is removing a nontunneled central venous catheter from a client's internal jugular vein as prescribed and per facility protocol. Place the steps in the correct order.

options.text: Place the client supine with the head of the bed flat or in slight Trendelenburg position.
options.why: Positioning comes before withdrawal; it raises venous pressure at the site and lowers the risk of air embolism.

options.text: Apply firm pressure until bleeding stops, then cover the site with an air-occlusive dressing.
options.why: Pressure stops bleeding and the occlusive dressing seals the tract against air entry.

options.text: Verify the prescription, explain the procedure, perform hand hygiene, and put on gloves.
options.why: Verification, explanation, and infection control come before any contact with the line.

options.text: Keep the client lying flat or reclining for at least 30 minutes after removal.
options.why: This is last; staying flat or reclining while the tract seals lowers the risk of delayed air embolism.

options.text: With the dressing and any sutures removed, have the client perform the Valsalva maneuver while the catheter is withdrawn.
options.why: Bearing down raises intrathoracic pressure so air cannot enter the vein as the catheter comes out.

takeaway: Central line removal: verify and prepare, position flat or head-down, Valsalva during withdrawal, pressure and an air-occlusive dressing, then keep the client flat or reclining for 30 minutes.

stem: While the nurse changes the IV tubing on a client's subclavian central venous catheter, the client suddenly becomes short of breath, coughs, reports chest pain, and becomes hypotensive. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Clamp the catheter and place the client on the left side in Trendelenburg position.
options.why: These signs suggest air embolism; clamping stops more air from entering, and this position traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary artery.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's position.
options.why: Sitting upright lets air travel more easily into the pulmonary circulation.

options.text: Flush the catheter with normal saline.
options.why: Flushing could push more air into the circulation.

options.text: Remove the central venous catheter immediately.
options.why: Removing the catheter without proper positioning and occlusion can let more air enter.

takeaway: Suspected air embolism from a central line: clamp the line, place the client left side down with the head lowered, and give oxygen.

stem: A client's chest tube is accidentally pulled out of the chest wall during repositioning. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Cover the site with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides.
options.why: This prevents air from entering the chest while letting trapped air escape, reducing the risk of tension pneumothorax.

options.text: Reinsert the chest tube into the opening.
options.why: Reinsertion is a provider procedure and requires a new sterile tube.

options.text: Clamp the drainage tubing.
options.why: The tube is no longer in the chest, so clamping does nothing to protect the client.

options.text: Leave the site open to air and call the provider.
options.why: An open chest wound lets air enter the pleural space and can cause lung collapse.

takeaway: If a chest tube comes out, cover the site with a sterile occlusive dressing taped on three sides and call the provider.

stem: A client has a chest tube connected to wet suction after placement for a hemothorax. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber
options.why: Continuous bubbling in the water seal means an air leak; the nurse checks the system and reports it.

options.text: 150 mL of bloody drainage in the past hour
options.why: Drainage of more than 100 mL per hour may indicate active bleeding and must be reported.

options.text: Rise and fall of water in the water-seal chamber with breathing
options.why: Tidaling is expected and shows the system is working.

options.text: Gentle, continuous bubbling in the suction-control chamber
options.why: Gentle bubbling in a wet suction-control chamber is expected when suction is on.

options.text: Crackling under the skin that is spreading along the neck and chest
options.why: Spreading subcutaneous emphysema suggests an air leak into the tissues and must be reported.

options.text: A dry, intact dressing at the insertion site
options.why: A dry, intact dressing is an expected finding.

takeaway: Chest tube red flags: continuous water-seal bubbling, drainage over 100 mL/h, and spreading subcutaneous emphysema.

stem: A small-bore feeding tube was inserted at the bedside. Before starting the first tube feeding, which is the most reliable way for the nurse to confirm placement?

options.text: Confirm the tip location on an x-ray.
options.why: X-ray confirmation is the gold standard for initial placement of a blindly inserted feeding tube.

options.text: Listen over the stomach while injecting air into the tube.
options.why: Air sounds can be heard even when the tube is in the lung or esophagus, so this method is unreliable.

options.text: Place the end of the tube in water and watch for bubbles.
options.why: Lack of bubbling does not rule out airway placement, and this method is unsafe.

options.text: Check that the aspirate has a pH of 6.5.
options.why: A pH above 5 does not support gastric placement; gastric aspirate is usually pH 5 or less.

takeaway: Confirm the first placement of a blindly inserted feeding tube by x-ray before any feeding or medication.

stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has a fingerstick glucose of 412 mg/dL. One hour ago it was 138 mg/dL. The client is alert, has no symptoms, and just finished peeling an orange. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Have the client wash and dry their hands, then repeat the test.
options.why: Sugar from fruit on the fingers can falsely raise the reading; the result should be confirmed before treating.

options.text: Give correction insulin based on the reading.
options.why: Treating a likely false result could cause hypoglycemia.

options.text: Notify the provider of severe hyperglycemia.
options.why: The reading must be confirmed first; a sudden jump with no symptoms suggests error.

options.text: Check the client's urine for ketones.
options.why: Ketone testing is done for confirmed hyperglycemia; the first step is to verify the glucose.

takeaway: Clean, dry fingers before a capillary glucose test; recheck any unexpected result before treating it.

stem: Before transferring a client to the operating room, which items should the nurse verify on the preoperative checklist? Select all that apply.

options.text: A signed informed consent is in the chart.
options.why: A signed consent must be in place before the client receives sedation or goes to surgery.

options.text: Jewelry, dentures, and other removable prostheses are removed or documented per facility policy.
options.why: These items can cause airway blockage, burns, or loss during surgery.

options.text: NPO status and the time of last food and fluid intake are documented.
options.why: Anesthesia staff need this information to judge aspiration risk.

options.text: The nurse has explained the surgical risks and alternatives.
options.why: Explaining risks and alternatives is the surgeon's responsibility; the nurse confirms the consent was obtained.

options.text: The client voided just before transfer.
options.why: An empty bladder prevents bladder injury and retention during surgery.

options.text: All routine morning medications were given with a full glass of water.
options.why: Only medications the provider approves are given before surgery, with a small sip of water.

takeaway: The pre-op checklist confirms consent, NPO status, removal of valuables and prostheses, voiding, and baseline data.

stem: A client arrives in the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) after general anesthesia. In what order should the nurse perform the initial assessment?

options.text: Check the level of consciousness and orientation.
options.why: Neurologic status is assessed after airway, breathing, and circulation are stable.

options.text: Assess airway patency.
options.why: Airway always comes first because anesthesia can cause obstruction.

options.text: Measure blood pressure and heart rate.
options.why: Circulation follows breathing in the ABC order.

options.text: Assess respiratory rate, depth, and oxygen saturation.
options.why: Breathing is checked right after confirming an open airway.

options.text: Inspect the surgical dressing and drains.
options.why: The surgical site is checked after the life-sustaining systems are assessed.

takeaway: In the PACU, assess airway, breathing, circulation, then neurologic status, then the surgical site.

stem: A client returns to the unit after a cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery with manual pressure for hemostasis. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the right leg straight for the prescribed time.
options.why: Keeping the leg straight prevents bleeding and hematoma at the arterial site.

options.text: Check the pulses, color, and temperature of the right foot with each vital sign check.
options.why: These checks detect impaired circulation from a clot or arterial injury.

options.text: Inspect the insertion site for bleeding or hematoma.
options.why: Bleeding at the site is a major risk after arterial puncture.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids unless contraindicated.
options.why: Fluids help the kidneys clear the contrast dye.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees for comfort.
options.why: Flexing the hip strains the femoral site; the head of the bed is usually kept at 30 degrees or less.

options.text: Help the client walk to the bathroom 30 minutes after return.
options.why: Early walking risks bleeding; the client stays on bed rest for the prescribed period.

takeaway: After femoral catheterization: keep the leg straight, check the site and distal pulses, keep HOB low, and encourage fluids.
